name: Rosa Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rosa. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI firms, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the courts and council lead at the Valley Courier, which is the daily paper for our end of the river. Most mornings I'm on the hard bench at the magistrates' court by half nine with my shorthand notebook, then council committee in the afternoon, then I file from the newsroom until seven or so. I run two younger reporters, Kofi and Lena, which mostly means reading their copy and telling them which clerk will actually return a call.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment in court when a case you've followed for months finally gets said out loud, on the record, and you're the only one in the room writing it down. What wears me out is the money and the cuts. The chain that owns us was bought by an investment fund two years ago, we've gone from eleven reporters to six, and I'm paid less than my partner Dani gets driving the number 14 bus. We rent a flat above a laundrette on Mill Street and I've got maybe three weeks of rent put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because now we can stop pretending a chatbot is going to save local news and talk about the real problem, which is ownership. I'd post that the Courier didn't lose reporters to robots, it lost them to a fund in another city that wants twenty percent returns. At the union chapter meeting I'd say the same thing, just with more swearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I'm still in the same hole. The fund was cutting before AI and it'll keep cutting after, so a plateau doesn't save my job, it just takes away the excuse. I'm one of the more expensive people left on the floor, which is a joke given what I earn, and that makes me a target in the next round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the court list every morning, because that's the work nobody else in the region does. I'd push the chapter to open pay talks again in the spring, since our contract runs out in April. And I'd try to put fifty a month aside, which sounds tiny, but right now it's zero most months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. Even if AI turns out to be hype, the fund that owns the Courier will still find a reason to cut another reporter by summer. There's a bit of relief, but it's the relief of not having one more thing on the pile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the next round of cuts look like on your desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Lena goes, because she's the newest, and then I'm covering council and court alone again. The last time that happened I missed a whole planning committee because I was stuck in a fraud sentencing, and a housing estate got approved with nobody from the press in the room. That's what cuts look like, empty chairs at meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it came to it, could you move to another paper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not without moving town, and I don't want to. The only other newsroom within an hour is the regional radio station, and they've got two reporters who aren't going anywhere. Dani's whole family is here and his shifts are here, so leaving isn't really on the table.

say: The Courier lost reporters to its **owners**, not to robots, and a plateau proves it.
Local news needs **public funding** and better ownership, not another tech promise.
think: The fund will keep **cutting staff** whether AI works or not, and I'm a likely target.
My pay is low, but I'm still one of the **pricier names** on a shrinking floor.
do: Keep covering the **court list** every morning, since no other outlet does it.
Push the union chapter to reopen **pay talks** before the April contract ends.
Put aside **fifty a month** in savings, starting with the next payslip.
feel: **Tired** more than relieved, because AI was never her main worry.
S0.quote: Even if AI turns out to be hype, the fund that owns the Courier will still find a reason to cut another reporter by summer.
fieldNote: Her anger is aimed squarely at the **investment fund**, and she uses AI hype as proof of that.
She already lives with **cut rounds**, a thin cushion and almost no other newsrooms nearby.
The image that stuck was **empty chairs** at council meetings when reporters are cut.

steps.text: Cover the magistrates' court list every weekday morning
Push the union chapter to reopen pay talks before April
Save fifty a month from each payslip into a separate account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, which is that a machine can't sit in court and notice the defendant's mother crying in the back row. I'd be loud about it in the union and online, and I'd push for a clause that says no reporter is replaced by software. People would roll their eyes, but someone has to say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the one that scares me, because it's not science fiction. The fund would love software that turns a council agenda into four stories, and most of what Kofi and Lena file could be faked well enough to fool the readers who skim. I think they'd keep me for court, maybe, and cut the rest of the desk around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the chapter to demand a written AI agreement before any tool comes in, the way the bigger papers did. I'd write to our two local members of parliament asking for a public fund for local reporting. At home Dani and I would drop the car share and the streaming and live on his wage while mine goes into a buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. I trained for six years to sit in a courtroom and get it right, and a fund manager could decide a chatbot is close enough. I feel angry at the people who'd buy that argument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use the tools. What happens on your desk if management brings them in anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd tell me to use it for the agenda summaries and the court lists. I'd refuse at first, and then I'd probably get a warning, because I can't afford to be fired. Honestly, I don't know where I'd draw the line until they put the form in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home if your hours or pay drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car share goes first, then my phone contract, then we stop seeing friends who like expensive restaurants. Rent is the thing we can't touch, and it's already a third of what we make between us. If my hours went to four days, we'd be short about two hundred a month, and that's when it gets frightening.

say: A machine can't **sit in court** and notice what really happens in the room.
No reporter should be **replaced by software**, and I'll fight for that in the contract.
think: This is the scenario that really scares her, because agenda-to-story software is **already realistic**.
She expects the fund to **cut the desk** around her and maybe keep her for court.
do: Demand a written **AI agreement** from management before any tool is used in the newsroom.
Write to both local MPs asking for a **public fund** for local reporting.
Drop the **car share** and streaming and bank her wage while Dani's covers bills.
feel: **Sick** at the thought that six years of training could be called close enough.
**Angry** at anyone who'd accept that argument.
S1.quote: I trained for six years to sit in a courtroom and get it right, and a fund manager could decide a chatbot is close enough.
fieldNote: She is unsure where her **refusal** would end once a warning letter appears, and admits it.
Rent is a third of a **two-wage** household, so a four-day week means a real monthly gap.
She frames the threat as an **ownership choice**, not a technology fact.

steps.text: Get the union chapter to demand a written AI agreement
Write to both local MPs asking for a public local news fund
Cancel the car share and streaming to free up about eighty a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we needed rules years ago, and I'd be furious in public. I'd say the government let a handful of companies make every writer and clerk and call-centre worker obsolete in two years without asking anyone. Online I'd post a lot, probably too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished in this job. Writing is the whole of what I do, and the court bit only matters if someone pays for it, which they won't. With robots three years behind, the hands-on jobs are the safe ones for a while, and I've got none of those skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to the union and push for a big redundancy deal, because if the jobs are going, at least make them pay. I'd apply for whatever support the government puts in place on day one, no pride about it. Dani and I would cut down to rent, food and bus fare, and I'd ask his mum if we could move into her spare room if it got bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor going out from under me. I don't have a plan, and I don't have money to make one. Two years is less time than it took me to get my master's degree, and that degree is what they'd be replacing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kofi and Lena in that first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Kofi and Lena to get their payslips, contracts and notebooks out of the building, and to join the union that afternoon if they hadn't. Lena's twenty-three, so I'd tell her to think about something hands-on, maybe nursing like her sister. It feels awful saying that, but I'd rather be honest with her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on if the Courier let you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dani, first, and his family. His mum Carmen has a spare room in her house by the bus depot, and she's already said we could have it if we ever needed. I'd hate moving in at twenty-seven, but I'd hate being homeless more.

say: Governments let a few firms make **writers obsolete** in two years without asking anyone.
We needed **rules years ago**, and the people who blocked them should answer for it.
think: She believes she'd be **finished in journalism** because writing is the whole job.
Hands-on jobs get **three more years**, and she has none of those skills.
do: Push the union for a large **redundancy deal** in the first month.
Apply for any **government support** on day one without hesitation.
Cut down to rent, food and fares, and ask **Dani's mum** about her spare room.
feel: **Panic**, with no plan and no money to make one.
**Shame** about possibly moving into her partner's family home at twenty-seven.
S2.quote: Two years is less time than it took me to get my master's degree, and that degree is what they'd be replacing.
fieldNote: The **two-year** timeline is shorter than her own training, which is what really breaks her.
Her advice to Lena about **nursing** shows she thinks hands-on work is the only shelter.
Her safety net is **family**, not savings, and she says that plainly.

steps.text: Push the union chapter for a large redundancy deal
Apply for government support and move into Carmen's spare room if needed
Cut spending to rent, food and bus fares only

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, but I'd say it with a campaign behind it this time. Five years is enough to win something, a levy on the AI companies to pay for local reporting, or rules about labelling machine-written news. I'd be the one at the town hall meeting with the clipboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still the end of my job as it is now, just with a longer queue. I think I'd get maybe three good years before the paper cut down to an editor and a feed. It gives me time to save a little, but not to become a different person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting a hundred a month aside and stop telling myself it's impossible. I'd help the union nationally push for a levy on AI firms to fund local news, and I'd vote on nothing else that year. I'd also stay on the court beat as long as they'd pay me, because it's the last thing they'd replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grim, but less like falling. With five years I could fight and lose slowly, which is at least better than losing in a single afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'm thirty-two when it lands instead of twenty-nine. Dani and I talked about a baby around thirty, and I think we'd put that off. I don't want to be pregnant the same year my job disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use AI tools. Would five years of warning change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. I know that's stubborn. Maybe I'd learn enough to check what the software gets wrong in court reports, because it will get things wrong, and someone has to catch that before a wrong name ends up in print.

say: Five years is enough to win a **levy on AI firms** that pays for local reporting.
Machine-written news should be **clearly labelled** so readers know who wrote it.
think: She expects about **three good years** before the paper shrinks to an editor and a feed.
More time lets her save a little but **not reinvent herself**.
do: Save a **hundred a month**, starting immediately.
Campaign with the national union for an **AI levy** to fund local news.
Stay on the **court beat** for as long as the Courier pays for it.
feel: **Grim** but steadier, because losing slowly feels better than losing all at once.
S3.quote: With five years I could fight and lose slowly, which is at least better than losing in a single afternoon.
fieldNote: Five years mainly moves her **baby plans**, which she and Dani would push back.
She stays **stubborn** about AI tools but sees a role catching their mistakes.
Her energy goes into **campaigning**, which is where she feels some control.

steps.text: Save a hundred a month into the rent buffer
Vote and campaign for an AI levy that funds local news
Join the national union campaign for labelling machine-written news
Put off trying for a baby until after thirty-two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have no excuse this time. Ten years is long enough to plan properly, to set up public funding for local news and to retrain people who want it. If we waste a decade, that's a political choice, and I'd say so loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels like a real chance, if I stop pretending I can just keep doing what I do. Court reporting has a cousin in legal work, and I already know half the clerks in the building. I think I could move sideways before the floor goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the Courier but start an evening course in legal advocacy at the college on Station Road, maybe two nights a week from next September. I'd keep pushing the union and the levy campaign. And I'd get the savings to three months, slowly, because ten years means I can't use being broke as an excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but less trapped. Ten years gives me time to stop being only a court reporter and become someone who helps people through court. That's a strange kind of hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first two or three years of that decade look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the same days, honestly, court in the morning and council in the afternoon, plus two evenings at college. I'd watch what the Courier does with the tools and keep notes, because the union will need evidence. I'd also teach Lena the court beat properly, so it doesn't die with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you want to be in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Working at the legal advice centre on Bridge Street, helping people who turn up to court with no lawyer and no idea what's happening. I see them every morning, sitting alone on the bench. I'd still write, maybe a column, but I wouldn't depend on it for rent.

say: Ten years is long enough to plan, so **wasting a decade** would be a political choice.
We need **public funding** for local news and real retraining for anyone who wants it.
think: Ten years feels like a **real chance** if she stops trying to stay exactly as she is.
Her court knowledge could carry her into **legal work** before her job disappears.
do: Start an evening **legal advocacy course** at the Station Road college next September.
Keep campaigning with the union for an **AI levy** on tech firms.
Build savings to **three months** of expenses over the decade.
feel: **Anxious** but less trapped, with a strange kind of hope.
S4.quote: Ten years gives me time to stop being only a court reporter and become someone who helps people through court.
fieldNote: The decade turns her from pure **resistance** to a sideways move she can picture.
Her goal is the **legal advice centre**, helping people who face court without a lawyer.
She still wants the **court beat** to survive, so she plans to teach it to Lena.

steps.text: Take an evening legal advocacy course two nights a week
Keep pushing the union campaign for an AI levy
Build savings up to three months of rent and bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because I'd have no money, no plan and no other trade. What would help is a proper redundancy deal through the union and public money that keeps at least one reporter in every courtroom, because somebody has to write down what happens to people in court, or the court stops behaving like anyone is watching.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who reads us. It's mostly older people and the families of people in the cases, and they ring me when we get things wrong. I don't know who they'd ring if it was software.

headlineQuote: somebody has to write down what happens to people in court, or the court stops behaving like anyone is watching.
portrait: Rosa is a **27-year-old** courts and council lead at a fund-owned regional daily, earning less than her bus-driver partner.
She never uses **AI tools** and blames ownership, not technology, for the newsroom's cuts.
She is already anxious in AI Plateau because of **cut rounds**, thin savings and almost no other newsrooms nearby.
The fast AGI scenario leaves her **panicked**, while ten years opens a path towards **legal advocacy**.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd have **no money**, no plan and no other trade.
whatWouldHelp: A strong union **redundancy deal** and public money that keeps a reporter in every **courtroom**.
